    WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

    Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, remarked organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

    “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell remarked, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”.

    “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also crucial to take advantage when it delivers,” she added.

    Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said.

    Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”.

    The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

    According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, mentioned the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

    “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she mentioned. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”.

    Recent findings suggest that and then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”.

    “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”.

    If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

    “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.”.

    Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah.

    Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total customers are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

    Sources indicate that all in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill mentioned. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

    According to recent reports, “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

    According to recent reports, two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

    Recent findings suggest that “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill remarked. “It always hits with the audience.”.

    Industry observers note that sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

    Security Engineer, Vulnerability Management at LiveKit

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
    • Recent findings suggest that our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end users, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk.
    • think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    Recent findings suggest that our customers trust us with audio, video and data belonging to their own end users, so a security failure on our side puts their data and their business at risk. We are hiring a Security Engineer to build and run our vulnerability management and security operations program. Vulnerability management is a core capability for keeping our security posture strong as the platform and the company grow: knowing what we run, finding what is exposed, and getting the right fixes shipped quickly. It also underpins our customer commitments and the compliance programs we are building. Our program is early, and you will shape it. You will join a small Trust team that covers security, IT and compliance, and you will own this program end to end from your first week.

    think like both a builder and a breaker, and understand security from first principles.

    take an automation-first and pragmatic approach to risk mitigation.

    translate security concerns into engineering action.

    can clearly explain complex technical concepts to others.

    are a fast learner and thrive in ambiguity.

    Select, deploy and operationalize scanning tooling across our production assets.

    Run vulnerability management end to end: triage, severity in our environment, owner assignment, remediation SLAs and reporting.

    Build engineering-first triage and remediation workflows that fit how our engineering teams already work, and automate the routing and follow-up.

    Build a remediation dashboard that engineering and leadership read and act on.

    Automate collection of the vulnerability management evidence our compliance programs depend on, in partnership with our Compliance team.

    Build automation, including agentic tooling, that removes manual security operations work and keeps pace with engineering growth.

    5+ years in security engineering, security operations or software engineering, with a significant share of that focused on security.

    Hands-on experience building or running a vulnerability management program or software security tooling (SCA, container, cloud or host scanning).

    An engineering-first approach to triage and remediation: you get findings fixed by making the fix easy to ship.

    The judgment to set a finding's real severity in our environment, using CVSS as one input.

    Strong scripting and automation skills in a language such as Go or Python, and comfort reading infrastructure as code such as Terraform.

    A pragmatic approach to risk: you can explain why a finding matters to the business and how fast it needs to be fixed.

    Experience with real-time media, networking or WebRTC systems.

    Experience supporting compliance audits such as HIPAA, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

    Incident response or application security experience.

    Experience in AI security, such as securing LLM applications or agent infrastructure.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    LiveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

    #101197. Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1272 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google’s Expansion Of Personal Intelligence Will Change SEO via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature.
    • Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.
    • Sources indicate that “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that google announced the expansion of its Personal Intelligence feature. The expansion unifies many of Google’s disparate products and services into a single personalized search experience. This upgrade represents a profound change to Google’s Search experience and is likely among the most consequential changes to SEO.

    Google’s announcement explains the connection to Search:.

    Sources indicate that “The most helpful search experience brings together the richness of the world’s information with insights uniquely relevant to you. Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence — and we’re introducing more personally relevant responses, so it’s easier to find just what you need.”.

    Some SEOs objected to characterizing Personal Intelligence as something that is about Search, explaining that Personal Intelligence is about Gemini, AI Mode, and AI Overviews. That view can be justified because Google’s announcement is somewhat ambiguous.

    It has been revealed that google’s announcement uses the upper-case word Search sixteen times. That seems to be a clear signal that Personal Intelligence affects Search.

    “A more tailored Google Search that’s uniquely yours….

    …Get more helpful Search responses….

    …Today, Search is getting even more tailored with the ability to connect more of your apps to Personal Intelligence….

    …bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

    The following passage seems to unambiguously paint the rollout as affecting Search:.

    “Starting to roll out today, you can opt in to securely connect Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, with support for Drive and the Gemini app following in the coming weeks — bringing context from your spending, documents, and chats directly to Search.”.

    The above passage clearly separates AI Mode from Search. Yet, other passages reference AI Mode in Search, introducing a certain amount of ambiguity. An argument can be made that this does not affect Search, but there’s a strong counter-argument there, too.

    Google’s announcement ties AI Overviews and AI Mode responses to recent Search contexts, meaning that contextual data from Search can be shared to AIO and AI Mode:.

    “You’ll also start seeing more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode, tailored to your recent search context.”.

    And in another passage Google explains that the contextual data from the Gemini App can be shared with AI Mode in Search:.

    “In the coming weeks you can easily share context across the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search.”.

    “So if you explore an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa.”.

    So it looks like the context data flows from Search to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as from the Gemini App to AI Mode in Search.

    The announcement identifies six connected apps:.

    According to recent reports, but Personal Intelligence is about a whole lot more. It’s about the transformation of disparate services and products into what Google CEO, Sundar Pichai, described in October 2026 as one unified search experience that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

    It has been revealed that “I expect our agents to provide that unifying experience across these products. In fact, that agentic layer, rather than try to converge or think about different products and how they come together, I think the agentic layer naturally ends up doing that, right?

    Because your agents, they’re running in the cloud, they’re running 24/7, they have your context. And so they can pick up things where you left off.

    Sources indicate that so you can start a task in some place. You go to the other place. Your agent has that context for you.

    So I think the agentic layer offers us a chance to bring a unified product experience better than ever before.”.

    Google’s Personal Intelligence was first revealed as a paid Gemini App beta feature in January 2026, which was expanded to AI Mode in search about a week later, initially supporting Gmail and Google Photos as an opt-in Search Labs experiment.

    In March it was expanded to free tier consumers in the United States and within a few months it was available in 200 countries and 98 languages.

    Industry observers note that google confirmed the expansion of the range of information AI Mode can draw on through Personal Intelligence so that now it includes Google Wallet data, files stored in Google Drive, and Gemini conversations. Google also announced increased personalization of AI Overviews and AI Mode based on recent search activity.

    According to recent reports, opt-in connectivity of Google Wallet to AI Mode is beginning to roll out. This is really substantial and ties into Sundar Pichai’s vision of Search becoming increasingly focused on helping people accomplish tasks. Google Wallet aggregates data from linked accounts like Gmail and partner apps.

    Google Wallet affects travel (like airline tickets), finance, commerce, event tickets, plus sensitive data (in some regions) like drivers license, and health insurance cards. When this feature is enabled, Google Wallet automatically scans incoming emails to import boarding passes, event tickets, loyalty cards, and shipping updates.

    Now all of that is connected with Personal Intelligence.

    Sources indicate that connectivity to AI Mode is coming in the next few weeks. Google announced that connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence will enable AI Mode to pull information from across stored Google Drive documents, spreadsheets, and PDFs to provide personalized responses and assist users with projects, planning, and decision-making.

    “With Google Drive connected in Personal Intelligence, you can get uniquely helpful responses that take all of that context into account and help you get started, like a personalized preparation plan ahead of tax season.”.

    Personal Intelligence will be sharing Gemini conversational context between the Gemini app and AI Mode within the next few weeks. Search personalization will come in the form of more personally relevant responses based on recent search activity.

    Industry observers note that personalization transparency is coming soon. Users will be able to see what personal context AI Mode used to generate a response and correct that information.

    Transformation Of Google Search Personal Intelligence represents a fundamental change in how Google Search (and/or AI Mode in Search) can respond to people, incorporating knowledge about their activities alongside information from the web.

    Unification Of Google’s Products And Services Previously disparate Google products and services are now increasingly part of a unified, personalized search experience.

    Google’s Agentic Layer The expansion of Personal Intelligence is consistent with Sundar Pichai’s vision of a unified, task-based experience that maintains context across Google’s products.

    Sharing Of Contextual Data The sharing of personal and conversational context across Google’s products enables users to continue activities without having to start over.

    Expansion Beyond Information Discovery The integration of additional data sources enables Google to become increasingly useful for planning, decision-making, and accomplishing tasks.

    Increasingly Personalized Search Experiences Search responses are becoming more specific to individual owners, a change that SEOs need to really think about and integrate into how what they do fits into this newly introduced multi-dimensional level of Search.

    How To Opt Out Of Google Personal Intelligence Google is giving users greater insight into and control over the personal context used to generate AI Mode responses. Users can opt out or in from Personal Intelligence here.

    Google Search is increasingly an experience that’s as much about what Google knows about the user and what they want to accomplish as it is about what the user is searching for. This is arguably one of the most consequential moments in SEO that I have experienced in my nearly 30 years of experience in SEO.

    Is “seen on the Orange Line” the newly introduced “overheard on the Acela”?

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEProPublica wanted to find more sources in the federal government. So it brought a truck.Neel DhaneshaMarch 31, 2025ProPublica reported on potential looks to overhaul the Smithsonian on Monday. Alec MacGillis and Andy Kroll wrote that the plans, if enacted, “would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.”.

    But how did MacGillis and Kroll get their hands on the explosive 25-item list? An open laptop, a crowded D.C. Metro train, and a quick-thinking tipster. From the ProPublica piece:.

    In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Initiative.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

    The ProPublica reporters, going off initials seen on the laptop, searched White House staffing records and “took to the Orange Line,” hoping it was a regular route for the staffer.

    Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint.

    Kroll told me that he and MacGillis made three trips to different parts of the Orange Line to report out the tip.

    “That included me standing outside for a few hours in a Metro station on an especially cold morning with a woefully insufficient coat on,” Kroll added. “Not the most glamorous reporting assignment, but important to getting the story.”.

    In a recent development, we’ve covered ProPublica’s creative attempts to reach prospective tipsters — which include an LED billboard truck and public transit ads in the Washington, D.C. area — in the past. The nonprofit investigative outlet has been a news industry leader in crowdsourcing and engagement reporting.

    In a recent development, proPublica engagement and tips coordinator Adriana Pera told me that the tips line has been “very, very busy.” In November, ProPublica received its “highest number of tips to date,” Pera stated. At least 20 ProPublica investigations in the last year started with sensitive information delivered through the tips line.

    RELATED ARTICLEHow to leak to a journalistLaura Hazard OwenApril 2, 2025“We have to attribute some of this surge to our efforts to get out into the world and show people that we’re listening and that they can trust us with their knowledge — from working with ad companies in Washington, D.C., to get our tips line on bus shelters, to flyering outside of conferences, and events with sources that could help our reporting needs,” she mentioned.

    Sources indicate that during a recent conference for the Association of the United States Army (AUSA), the largest annual gathering of Army contractors, Pera and others handed out flyers. ProPublica also purchased ads on bus shelters they thought attendees were likely to walk by.

    Recent findings suggest that “We’re always looking for ways to reach the people we need to reach, in the places they’re likeliest to be, based on our reporting needs,” Mel Kramer, engagement team product manager, said. “A good tips line is both staffed and comes to mind quickly. When someone sees something that investigative reporters should see, we want them to think of ProPublica.”.

    It has been revealed that up next for the team? Handing out coasters in sports bars to collect info on sports betting.

    #101190. Bing’s AI Cites Support Pages, PDFs & Staff Bios – 883,313 Citations Analyzed via @sejournal, @dodgejd

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2857 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Bing’s AI Cites Support Pages, PDFs & Staff Bios – 883,313 Citations Analyzed via @sejournal, @dodgejd

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that in February, Bing released the public preview of its AI Performance Reporting function inside Webmaster Tools.
    • Recent findings suggest that blog posts, product pages, and homepages account for less than half of the citations in our sample, 42% combined.
    • Recent findings suggest that the single most cited URL in our data set was an app page for a consumer product with an integrated mobile app component.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in February, Bing released the public preview of its AI Performance Reporting function inside Webmaster Tools. Since then, we have been using it to gauge a bit more insight into what Bing is citing and what might be impacting those results. Monitoring different sites since then, we set out to analyze more than 883,000 AI citations across 26 brands, which surfaced a few things that may surprise you.

    Recent findings suggest that blog posts, product pages, and homepages account for less than half of the citations in our sample, 42% combined. The other 58% is a mix of app pages, attractions lists, instruction manuals, course catalogs, key personnel directors, and PDFs that nobody on a content team was likely thinking about.

    Recent findings suggest that the single most cited URL in our data set was an app page for a consumer product with an integrated mobile app component. The second was an attractions list for a tourism destination organization.

    There certainly are other tools out there at the disposal of SEOs that help us understand what AI citations might look like, but at the time, this data was reported out of the only first-party tool inside of a search engine to do so. As soon as access was provided in February, we pulled AI reports for 15 different brands and published our findings. Since then, Microsoft has added query-to-page mapping, intent and topic labels, Citation Share, and a Topics Portfolio beta. They have also backfilled much of the underlying data from previous months’ releases, allowing us to pull data for the same 15 brands, plus an additional batch to spot any gaps or trends.

    Understanding semantic differences between searchers and the fact that all of the data inside the AI Reporting is sampled to some extent, we started with the page-level reporting instead of queries. Across most sites, the pages export will provide you with a broader data set to work from, also moving you past the common practitioner question, which is “what are people prompting,” when we set out to try and better understand “what on my site does the machine actually use?”.

    We explored the AI reports from 26 different brands across nine verticals. Included were destination marketing organizations, resorts and hoteliers, ecommerce brands, B2B manufacturers, colleges and universities, an EdTech platform, regional healthcare providers, government-adjacent business services, and a financial institution.

    Recent findings suggest that inside the AI Reporting portion, we exported the three report views for each brand: Grounding Queries, Cited Pages, and the Daily Overview. By the numbers, our overview totals delivered over 1.1 million citations across the brands, with over 883,000 on 10,861 URLs and a grounding query export of nearly 300,000 citations across 2,797 queries.

    Recent findings suggest that grounding queries are the search phrases Microsoft’s AI generates to retrieve content, not the words users type, and Microsoft states grounding query data “represents a sample of overall citation activity.” Pulling data from the fall shows us how much of a sample. Meaning that for every brand we reviewed, the query export sums to between 5% and 39% of the overview total, and the page export is between 63% and 100%. That is why we used page counts rather than queries for pattern spotting.

    It has been revealed that two additional rules were held in the course of our analysis. First, no raw-count comparisons were used across the periods. Knowing Microsoft backfilled AI Performance data from June 1, 2026, Krishna Madhavan described the resulting jumps as “just regular data backfilling” on X. Second, the two data pulls cover different seasons, and we only carried forward the findings that held up across both, spring and fall, and set aside the ones that seasonality could explain.

    See also: Microsoft Clarity Now Highlights Grounding Queries Behind AI Citations.

    Across all 883,313 page citations, grouped by what the page is for:.

    It has been revealed that as one might expect, pooled numbers are leaning toward big sites, and the median brand across the data looks quite different. Product and service pages accounted for 32%, whereas editorial content was 15%, homepage 8%, and everything else thereafter was much smaller.

    According to recent reports, citations appear to be fairly concentrated. Across the whole set, just over 2% of the URLs carry half of all citations. Breaking this down even more, we noted that it takes 1,441 URLs in our data to reach 80%. For a typical brand, the top page alone accounts for 12.7% of its citations and takes about 40 pages to reach 80% citation volume. As conversational search continues to grow, SEOs understand that the long-tail queries are expanding, but most of what Bing’s AI pulls from is a handful of pages.

    Recent findings suggest that across destination marketing organization websites, events and things-to-do pages remain nearly 50% of the citations, and listing directories make up another 15%, with lodging-related pages falling in at under 1%. The single biggest anomaly that stood out was a tourism attraction list with nearly 17,000 citations. Grounding queries are highly seasonal, with major events and festivals delivering a large share of the citations. What does this mean for destination marketers? The sites are highly sought after and relied upon for things to do, see, and experience, though less likely for the actual places to stay.

    Recent findings suggest that wanting to explore more lodging-oriented searches, we added in additional resort and hotelier properties where heads in beds is a primary function of their business. Lodging and reservations pages account for 4.3% of citations across resorts, wherein activities-related content such as golf, ski, dining, and packages pages account for nearly 50% of the citations. While one resort was cited for instructional content around golf techniques, regional golf trips were more likely to garner the results that generate positive conversations in the boardroom. What does this mean for resorts and hoteliers? Monitoring these trends over the course of a season, be it summer or winter, allows a resort to see the activity mix that rotates with the calendar. It’s worth noting that a resort (not a hotel) is cited as a place that does something, and almost never as just a place to sleep.

    Industry observers note that no surprise to anyone developing SEO strategies for ecommerce brands, product and category pages account for 40% of the citations, with support and documentation-related pages residing at 26%, and specific app/login pages making up nearly 20% of the citations. Stripping out the one brand whose app page is the most cited URL in our study, the product pages rise to 64% of the citations. A second brand that pairs a physical product with an app and a service strategy reveals the same shape. Its service plan and product support pages are two of its top three cited URLs, and PDF instruction manuals sit in its top 10. For brands that are focused on the growth of their app-enabled products, this means reviewing how you are positioned to own the support conversation. Similar to traditional search, AI models appear to be just fine citing your PDF documents, which leads to a poor customer experience and puts you down a path of hard-to-patch legacy content.

    Recent findings suggest that the closer a B2B brand is to the solution being delivered, the better. Across the brands reviewed, editorial content accounted for 46% of the citations. At one manufacturing services brand with a global presence, over 70% of the citations were URLs from technical how-to articles. The same can be remarked for training and tutorial-based content, especially video libraries, which accounted for 73% of citations. The exception to that is a product manufacturer whose catalog pages account for over 70% of the citations and another 10% for product literature PDFs. Meaning, if you are in the business of making highly specialized and technical products, the machine is just as happy sourcing its answers from a PDF, though again it causes more friction on the side of the customer and content teams who have to manage legacy updates over time.

    Sources indicate that academic programs, admissions-related pages, and financial aid make up nearly 40% of the citations for the higher ed vertical. From there, it filters out into reference material and course handouts at 13%; support and IT-related pages also at 13%; editorial articles come in at 12%, with faculty and about pages at 11%. For colleges and universities, the bulk of the pages being cited fall into more of an information-gathering category around what courses are offered, when, and the financial implications. For those working in academia, specifically higher ed, reviewing which of your pages are being referenced the most should start to provide you with insights on what your audience is seeking. If you’re a university that’s built on research and studies, there are clear signals that optimizing who your people are is a critical step that is potentially overlooked.

    Recent findings suggest that across the verticals reviewed, three categories surfaced that no content calendar is presently accounting for, and why would it? Noting PDF documents account for over 6% of all citations in total. Within the EdTech platform we reviewed, they account for nearly 17% of citations, with course catalogs also following a similar trend. Within one university, PDFs were 11% of their citations, surfacing elements from not just the course catalog but also core requirements that students need by program. Certainly, if you’re looking to own more of the conversation around your programs and what students can expect vs. letting the AI base it off of outdated PDFs, this is a prime opportunity to take action.

    At one ecommerce brand, PDFs were 10.4% of all citations, all of them instruction manuals. This serves as a reminder that if a PDF is the best document you have on a subject, it could very well be cited as the best document you have on the matter itself. For brands with products that require technical support, while revising a single PDF might seem like the approach to take, consider how many PDF documents are residing in your CMS that are outdated vs. placing the actual helpful information in an HTML format on your site.

    The homepages of many websites don’t go unnoticed in our review. Homepages are 6.8% of all citations pooled, and the homepage is the single most cited page for nine of the 26 brands reviewed. When nothing else on a site carries deeper insights about the brand, its services or products, the homepage is carrying a much higher share of the citations. It doesn’t matter the size of the brand either; that’s a signal that is worth reviewing to help you determine what the AI is thinking about your brand.

    Across healthcare, education, and EdTech, people and about pages carry between 4% and 11% of citations by vertical, and 18% at one university. When the AI answer is related to who you are as a brand or an individual, where you are located, and the key individuals who work there, these pages become critical elements when directing the LLMs. How many of these page types get published once, only to never be revisited and kept up to date?

    According to recent reports, looking back to an early study we did on the insights on what Bing’s Webmaster Tools was telling us about AI Citations, we revisited 15 of the original brands to determine what shifted over the course of time. Most of what moved was seasonal, and based on that, we decided to leave those elements out. However, we did find three areas worth investigating further.

    Industry observers note that in our original review in February, login, portal, and sign-in queries accounted for approximately 18% of all citations across the brands. In the fall window, that shrunk to just above 1%.

    Sources indicate that within the higher education sector, 45% of the citations originally came from login and portal queries. As we observed this shift into the fall, the same number of grounding queries had dropped to just shy of 1%. Login queries for the EdTech brand also dropped from 17% to less than 1%. And while there certainly is the seasonal argument to be made, we can look at August through October as being key times at most universities and colleges as the start of a semester. We expect institutional login lookups to increase around that time, and in fact, they did not.

    It has been revealed that product support for the ecommerce brands went the other direction, with one brand’s support and access-related content rising from 17% to 42% of its citations. Noting that fall is the peak season for the brand and that demand is trending exactly where you might expect it to be.

    Recent findings suggest that bing’s June patch added intent labels to the reporting, with Navigational among them. The February login queries are exactly what that label would catch. It also would appear that Microsoft has not said it suppresses AI answers differently across intent types, and what we are describing is more of a pattern to spot and not a mechanism within the report.

    For the median brand, only 37% of the citations found in our February review came from query strings that still appear in the fall export, and that is before accounting for any seasonal shifts. Across each of the brand’s top ten queries this spring, we note that approximately 56% are completely absent from the fall data pull. If your brand operates around any cyclicality where it is impacted by major events, holidays, or even seasonal activities, that explains some of the difference but not all.

    In a recent development, across the original data pull in February, we found a handful of location-only queries. Those that included [events near me], [concerts near me], and [holiday events near me], without a destination even in the query string, were present. Revisiting the same brands this fall, we see that the near me query left the data. Noting many of the AI-generated search results are favoring sites such as Eventbrite, Ticketmaster, and similar aggregator sites. The more local and regional focused your brand is, such as a multi-location storefront, the location-based data is going to be stronger and likely in line with what you experience in traditional search.

    We continue to see branded searches spread into the AI Overviews in Google, yet the data coming out of Google is still not as detailed as we would like. Within Bing, we do get a view into Citation Shares, which was added in June. This reports on the percentage of citations your site receives out of all citations shown for a grounding query, which should help you determine how much of the answer your brand actually holds.

    According to recent reports, citation Share is Bing’s measure of how much of an answer your site has supplied. For each grounding query, it reports what percentage of all citations shown for that query pointed to your pages. On branded queries, the sites in our analysis supplied 67% of the citations, and other sites supplied 33%. On non-branded queries, the sites supplied 25% and other sites supplied 75%. Compare this to your traditional search results and determine how much your branded searches are triggering AI-generated results.

    Non-branded searches tend to always be the opportunity in traditional search, and AI-generated results are certainly no different. The data in our most recent series of exports confirms this. On a non-branded query, three of every four citations are going to someone else.

    Industry observers note that up front, know that the data is all sampled, but likely the best we have to work with at the moment. The pipeline is constantly backfilling, so an increase across a three-month time period could indicate more usage, more backfill on recent dates, or both. Right now, the recommendation is to use the data as a guide and report on what the dashboard reveals rather than calling it growth.

    According to recent reports, overall, Bing’s intent labels hold up well, though it could be argued that their topic labels do not yet. Our review showed one consumer product brand filed under “Home Security Systems” for 57% of its citations. Microsoft’s June post allows that labels “may be broad” for niche domains, so plan on re-sorting them yourself. It’s also worth noting that not every grounding query traces back to a person. Queries of seven or more words grew from 1% of citations in February to 3% this fall, and some of them are plainly monitoring tools running on a schedule. Citation counts in any tool will include machine-initiated queries, and no report separates those out right now.

    Industry observers note that while Google remains the top in regards to search volume, the data coming out of their AI insights reporting is lackluster. Bing remains one of the better sources for a site owner to gauge first-party insights on what gets cited. Just be sure you read it for what it is: a sampling of your brand’s data. Have you found Bing’s AI Performance Report to be beneficial?

    Newsletters, obits, and the world’s longest yard sale: How some local news sites saw their traffic spike

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Big gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Big gainers included W42ST, the Point/Plover Metro Wire, Grice Connect (“In the rural south, death is a large social driver”), and the Philomath News. Here’s our quarterly ranking of the top 25 local for-profit news sites in the United States.

    Sources indicate that it’s time for our latest look at which newsrooms are having success increasing their web traffic. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, public media stations, and for-profit local news sites. Rankings are based on estimates from Similarweb.

    Recent findings suggest that today’s edition looks at local for-profit news sites. (Eligible sites for this ranking are for-profit members of the trade group LION Publishers — LION standing for Local, Independent, Online News — so these are mostly digital-born newsrooms, not newspapers or TV stations.) The rankings for Q3 feature many of the same sites that performed well in our last edition. This time around, we’ve got details from local news sites in Latest York, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nevada, Georgia, and Oregon. Below that are the Top 25 rankings for July, August, and September.

    According to recent reports, W42ST In Upcoming York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July. Publisher Phil O’Brien stated that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The New York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST. “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.” O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s right now trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The new daily newsletter they’ve debuted earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week. It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said. Point/Plover Metro Wire Wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski. The site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said. Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining new customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said. “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she said. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.” Grice Connect Statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July. DeWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position. But Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site. Philomath News The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath. Similarweb stats revealed a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he said. In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we launched in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said. Oklahoma City Free Press, LINK nky, This Is Reno In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.” The Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews. Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.     According to recent reports, in New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, W42ST has been covering neighborhood news since 2014. Its traffic jumped 84% from June to July.

    Publisher Phil O’Brien remarked that boost is attributable to one day’s traffic to a single story: this story on the deaths, four days apart, of Jeffrey Newman and Jayson Conner, a couple who ran Backpacks for the Street, a charity that offered supplies to those living on the city’s streets. W42ST published its story on July 11; a few hours later, The Newly introduced York Times ran its own obituary, and thousands of people who read that piece went to Google to find out more. Visits on July 12 were roughly 10 times a normal Sunday on W42ST.

    Industry observers note that “A spike like this is lovely, but it doesn’t pay the bills,” O’Brien told me over email. He noted that the average reader of that story who came from search was engaged for 26 seconds; readers who came to it from W42ST’s own newsletter averaged more than three and a half minutes. “A reader from across the country who spends 26 seconds on an obituary is welcome, but they’re not who we’re building for.”.

    O’Brien was writing to me from England, where he’s at the moment trying to bring W42ST’s hyperlocal model to the town of Southport (O’Brien was born in Liverpool). Stand Up For Southport is a six-year-old site that received a government Local News Fund grant to expand operations, and O’Brien is spending a few months there to offer his W42ST-bred expertise. The fresh daily newsletter they’ve launched earned more than 1,000 subs in the first week.

    It’s a nice reversal from just four years ago, when O’Brien had his American visa renewal application rejected because immigration officials declared W42ST was a “marginal” business. He spent the next five months running the site from London. “The idea is a hyperlocal model that can travel,” he said.

    In a recent development, wisconsin’s Point/Plover Metro Wire describes itself as the only locally owned and operated daily news source in Portage County, and the county is the only place it covers. “We do this mainly because nobody else here does, even if it does limit our audience,” said publisher Brandi Makuski.

    Recent findings suggest that the site had one of the largest leaps in July traffic of any in our rankings, up 114% from the month before. Makuski said high-performing stories in July included a proposed ban on homelessness, a stabbing homicide related to an eviction process, and an increase in stormwater rates for residents. “The extensive follow-up coverage on these and other stories has really helped expand our readership, and kind of reconnect in readers’ minds the importance of community journalism,” she said.

    Makuski said that about 63% of the site’s traffic comes from Facebook (“as much as I hate to say this…social media is the bane of my existence”). She describes much of her work as “public education” to convince businesses and institutions that a Facebook-first approach for getting the word out comes with risk. “We’re making headway and gaining upcoming customers each time, but it’s grueling piecemeal work,” she said.

    “We just do the work, and we’re pretty old-school,” she mentioned. “The scanner is on 24/7; we meet with municipal and industry leaders in person regularly; we constantly cultivate relationships and new sources; and, most importantly, we don’t sit on our asses. We spend about 75 percent of our workday, every day, out in the community, stumbling on most of our news in the field.”.

    Recent findings suggest that statesboro, Georgia, is a town of about 33,000, perhaps best known to Allman Brothers fans. The husband-and-wife team of DeWayne and Lori Grice have run Grice Connect since 2019. Their traffic was up about 77% from June to July.

    Sources indicate that deWayne Grice told me that Facebook and Google were both up notably. July was also the first full month the site had a full-time sports reporter, a Report for America-funded position.

    In a recent development, but Grice also credited its obituaries: “In the rural south, death is a large social driver.” During the COVID pandemic, he noticed that some deaths were going unrecorded in the local newspaper’s obit section; the paper charged $150 and up to run one, and they were behind a paywall. Grice Connect launched free obituaries, sponsored by a local hospice and in collaboration with five local funeral homes. Obits drove more than 44,000 views in July and were a “primary pillar” of the site.

    The Philomath News was founded in 2020 by publisher Brad Fuqua, two months after he’d been laid off by the Corvallis Gazette-Times when it closed its weekly paper in suburban Philomath.

    Similarweb stats indicated a 52% increase in the site’s traffic in September, though Fuqua tells me it was October when traffic really jumped. Interestingly, the site’s top referrer in September was NewsBreak, not Google. “Google came back in October, but September showed me how much it helps to have a second big source of traffic when search dips,” he noted.

    In a town as small as Philomath (pop. 5,500), Fuqua has had to figure out ways to drive some traffic from elsewhere in Oregon. He does so with his weekly writeups of the Oregon State Police logs, which he called “consistently my best-performing content” beyond the homepage and which attract readers from Portland and beyond. But it’s the local stories that are the reason the site exists. “People here have stuck with us since we rolled out in 2020, and that loyalty is what makes a one-person local news operation possible,” he said.

    In Oklahoma’s capital, traffic to the Free Press in July was up 68% from June. Editor-in-chief Brett Fieldcamp attributed that to an unusually high number of homicides that month (“we report, track, and number every homicide that is logged in OKC throughout the year”). But some of the site’s biggest individual traffic drivers were actually republished press releases from local governments and organizations. “If there’s any insight to glean or to communicate to your readers,” he told me, “it’s that curating and running press releases from trusted departments and local partners can be a far bigger driver of traffic at times than most people might realize, and also a great way to stay engaged with the community you serve.”.

    In a recent development, the Northern Kentucky site LINK nky saw its traffic jump 81% in July, which CEO Lacy Starling attributed to two stories. A routine unbylined piece on the World’s Longest Yard Sale — which “spans approximately 690 miles across six states” — pulled in 18,000 unique visitors, 10% of the site’s total traffic that month. Another piece on a fitness instructor who survived a “widow-maker” heart attack “must have been shared into a group or a site somewhere,” because it drove another 10,000-plus pageviews.

    Nevada’s This Is Reno had a strong August, up 71% from July. Publisher Bob Conrad attributed that to a frequent cause of local traffic spikes, a natural disaster — in their case, a series of wildfires, culminating in the devastating Hawk Fire.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    According to recent reports, the generational edge that reveals up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

    Ask a 19-year-old how TikTok decides what to show them, and you’ll likely get a fast, confident answer about watch time, likes, and how “the algorithm just gets me.” Ask their grandmother, and you’re more likely to get a shrug.

    The scene fits a story we’ve been telling for years: Young people are “digital natives” who intuitively grasp the platforms they grew up on, while older adults are outsiders, left behind and vulnerable. That story matters more than it used to. Algorithmically curated platforms are now a major source of news for Americans of all ages, which means people’s sense of how those systems work shapes how they judge the information they get there.

    But when you test what each group actually knows, rather than what they say they know, the story doesn’t hold up.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLETrapped by what they know: Young adults’ algorithmic cynicismMyojung ChungNovember 17, 2025In a piece last year for Nieman Lab, I reported that young adults who spent more time on social media tended to know less about how algorithms work, and I speculated that constant use might create an illusion of understanding. My recent study published in Latest Media & Society set out to test that idea directly — measuring not just what people know, but how confident they are about it — across the full adult age range.

    It has been revealed that surveying 1,205 U.S. adults ages 18 to 65 and older, I measured two things. First, I asked people to rate their own understanding of how algorithms select, rank, and personalize content. Second, I measured their actual awareness of how these systems work, which covers content filtering, automated decision-making, data use, and algorithmic bias.

    Recent findings suggest that the self-ratings matched the conventional wisdom: Younger respondents rated their understanding significantly higher than older respondents did. But the awareness scores did not. Across every age group, actual awareness of how algorithms function was essentially flat.

    Sources indicate that in other words, the generational edge that reveals up when you ask people how well they understand algorithms isn’t a knowledge edge. It’s a confidence edge.

    Recent findings suggest that to capture this, I use the concept “algorithmic knowledge confidence”: the gap between what people believe they know and what they can demonstrate. When self-assessment outpaces actual awareness, that’s overconfidence; when it lags behind, that’s underconfidence. Young adults tended toward the former: They don’t necessarily understand algorithms better, but they feel more certain that they do. Older adults tended toward the latter: They don’t know less, but they’re more cautious about claiming what they know.

    In a recent development, then why would the most-online generation feel the surest? Psychologists have long documented that people mistake familiarity for understanding. When something feels easy to process — often simply because we’ve encountered it many times — we tend to assume we understand it. This is called processing fluency.

    It has been revealed that exposure to social media differs sharply by age. About 95% of 18- to 29-year-olds use YouTube and about 63% use TikTok, according to Pew Research; among adults 65 and older, those figures drop to 64% and 12%. For younger customers, algorithmic feeds are part of the daily routine, and that routine produces a comfortable sense of “I know how this works,” whether or not it’s true. Older adults, with less exposure, don’t get the same fluency cues, and default to more conservative self-assessments.

    According to recent reports, my data are consistent with this explanation. The number of platforms people used daily accounted for a meaningful share of the link between age and overconfidence: The more platforms someone used, the further their self-rated understanding outran their demonstrated awareness. Because this is a survey taken at one point in time, it can’t prove that heavy use causes overconfidence, but the pattern fits the fluency account well.

    This miscalibration isn’t just a matter of bruised egos or modest grandparents. It highlights up in how people evaluate the news and information in their feeds.

    RELATED ARTICLEWant to fight misinformation? Teach people how algorithms workMyojung ChungSeptember 4, 2024Younger adults who overestimated their algorithmic understanding were more likely to see the content in their feeds as reliable and trustworthy, and more likely to believe they were being exposed to a diverse range of viewpoints. Older adults who underestimated their understanding showed the opposite pattern: more skepticism about the reliability of what they saw, and a sense that their feeds were narrower than they might actually be.

    Other research points in the same direction for younger audiences. A Stanford study found that two-thirds of U.S. high school students couldn’t tell a news article from sponsored content, a reminder that growing up inside algorithmic feeds is no guarantee of being able to evaluate them.

    But the older adults’ pattern isn’t a healthy one either. Blanket distrust is as poor a guide to information as blanket confidence. It can lead people to dismiss accurate reporting along with misinformation, or to disengage from platforms entirely rather than learning to use them critically.

    First, algorithmic literacy needs to teach calibration, not just content. Most digital literacy efforts focus on pouring in more information about how algorithms work. My findings suggest that’s only half the job. The other half is helping people accurately judge what they don’t know.

    Second, interventions should look different for different audiences. For younger, overconfident users, that might mean exercises designed to puncture false certainty: quick self-assessments that reveal the gap between what someone assumes and what they can actually explain, or interactive demonstrations of common misconceptions about how feeds are built. For older, underconfident users, the goal isn’t to manufacture confidence. It’s to help them recognize the caution they already bring to online information as a genuine strength, and to pair it with the skills to tell trustworthy sources from untrustworthy ones, so that skepticism becomes discernment rather than disengagement.

    In a recent development, third, anyone trying to reach audiences through algorithmic platforms, from educators to newsrooms to the platforms themselves, should stop assuming that the youngest users are the savviest. Confidence and competence are different things, and treating one as a proxy for the other leaves both groups poorly served.

    The next time a young adult confidently explains “how the algorithm works,” it might be worth asking: How can you be sure you actually know that? And the next time an older relative shrugs and indicates they don’t think they get it, it might be just another kind of miscalibration — with costs of its own, just a quieter one.

    Myojung Chung is an associate professor of journalism and media innovation at Northeastern University.

    The Wall Street Journal joins a growing list of publishers disallowing bots by default

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Many publishers are responding to a latest reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Many publishers are responding to a latest reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.

    Sources indicate that one of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The new bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

    It has been revealed that as part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

    Industry observers note that “As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” stated Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”.

    The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent tech giant, News Corp.

    According to recent reports, “We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” said Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”.

    Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

    An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents shows that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

    Recent findings suggest that many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the organization’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

    “One of the most important concerns for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson stated in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”.

    More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

    In a recent development, people Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

    Industry observers note that many of these publishers are responding to a newly introduced reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

    It has been revealed that despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The firm started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

    Known Agents right now tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

    “Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” stated King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”.

    King acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

    Sources indicate that “It’s been such a manual process,” noted King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”.

    Slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the organization’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

    Recent findings suggest that “We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, stated. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”.

    Lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he noted.

    Slate currently has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

    “It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” stated Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [revision your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”.

    • Recent findings suggest that google’s November 2026 core update finished rolling out on Nov.
    • In a recent development, the dashboard’s latest entry, posted at 6:03 a.m.
    • Glenn Gabe, SEO and AI Search Consultant at G-Squared Interactive, dates the update’s impact to Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that google’s November 2026 core update finished rolling out on Nov. 24, according to the Search Status Dashboard, putting the first post-update week Google suggests comparing in Search Console on U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

    In a recent development, the dashboard’s latest entry, posted at 6:03 a.m. PT, reads: “The rollout was complete as of November 24, 2026.” The revision began rolling out Nov. 10, so it finished inside the two-week window Google gave at launch, which I covered that day.

    Glenn Gabe, SEO and AI Search Consultant at G-Squared Interactive, dates the update’s impact to Nov. 13, three days after the rollout began. In a Nov. 17 post on X, he wrote that he believed the update “landed on Friday the 13th,” with Search Console showing big surges and drops for affected sites starting that day.

    Gabe leaned on Search Console because third-party SEO tools were “all over the place due to poisoning, filtering, etc.” By Nov. 20, he mentioned the tools’ trend lines matched what he saw in Search Console for those sites.

    Lily Ray, Founder of Algorythmic and VP, SEO & AI Search at Amsive, shared a chart on LinkedIn on Nov. 23 showing subfolders and subdomains on six sites that “have been dropping fast since Google’s November core patch started.” Each folder held one template repeated thousands of times, such as a page per word, per area code or per “X vs Y” word pairing. She wrote that most of the folders target searches “not closely related to the business offering.”.

    It has been revealed that ray wrote that within each site, “the content section (blog, resources, etc.) is falling hard while the main product/brand pages stay strong.” She has seen AI Overview and AI Mode citations to those folders “show similar drops” too. Her chart uses SISTRIX visibility data, with the same trend lines checked in Ahrefs, and doesn’t name the sites.

    Ray called these “fresh examples of the exact same SEO issues that have been hurting sites during core updates for years.” In an Oct. 7 column for SEJ, she listed templated, programmatic pages among the patterns she’d found on sites hit by Google updates this year.

    Google’s recommendations for core updates suggest waiting until at least a full week after an update has finished rolling out, then trying to compare a week of data post-rollout, Nov. 25 to Dec. 1 on this update’s dates, to a week of data pre-rollout such as Nov. 3-9.

    For retail sites, the week prior to the rollout will include regular traffic while the week immediately following the rollout includes Black Friday and may reflect holiday traffic. Another check would be comparing the same holiday traffic from last year alongside Google’s suggested comparative week.

    Industry observers note that marie Haynes wrote for SEJ that the click spike some site owners were seeing in their Search Console from Oct. 31-Nov. 2 wasn’t human traffic. A baseline start date of Nov. 3 excludes those days. There is also a logging concern listed on Google’s data anomalies page that resulted in lower impression counts in the Generative AI performance report for Nov. 9-11, which coincides with the end of the baseline week.

    It has been revealed that using a page path filter in the Performance report allows you to isolate your product pages and compare these to a templated content folder as described by Ray. Google’s guidance also says to avoid making changes to content that’s already performing well.

    The first full week after completion ends Dec. 1, so the comparison Google suggests can run once that day’s data reaches Search Console. Gabe wrote on Nov. 20 that tremors and reversals “can always happen as Google updates additional core systems” or spots something off in its results after an update.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Director of Technology Partnerships to lead the teams responsible for growing Supabase through technology integrations and our marketplace ecosystem.

    You’ll bring together two complementary motions: partnerships that embed Supabase into the products developers already use, and a marketplace that helps developers discover and connect complementary technologies to their Supabase projects. Your job is to turn both into durable sources of revenue, adoption, and customer value.

A central part of the role is working closely with AI labs to build strategic relationships, develop integrations, and bring joint opportunities to market. You’ll partner closely with Product, Engineering, Sales, Marketing, and Finance to take integrations from idea to launch—and grow their impact long after launch.
